title: Anthropomorphism: Constraint or Affordance in Mentor Prompts?
author: Terry Yu
summary: Drawing on a 2024 research project with English teacher Nick Potkalitsky, Terry Yu examines a subtle but consequential design flaw in AI mentor prompts: inadvertent anthropomorphism. Reviewing prompts he wrote two years ago, Yu notices verbs like 'establish rapport' and 'authentic interest' that project human capacities onto the AI—capacities it genuinely lacks—and concludes he slipped into anthropomorphism not as a design principle but as a 'prompt production fallacy.' He distinguishes mentor prompts (curriculum-embedded, teacher-assessable, task-specific, updated with lesson plans) from tutorials (topic-driven, modular, autonomous), arguing the former require far more careful engineering. Yu's evolving remedy is to reframe the AI as 'an audience with extremely limited capabilities,' directing it to perform rapport rather than feel it, and to leverage what AI actually does well—sentiment analysis, systematic language pattern recognition—rather than what a human mentor would do. Two detailed sample prompts designed for a university humanities course illustrate these principles in practice: one surfaces student assumptions about religion before the course begins; the other prepares students to read The Golden Ass without dismissing ancient magic as fantasy. The piece functions as both research note and craft essay, documenting thinking-in-progress about how our framing of AI shapes what we ask it to do and how well it can do it.
points: Mentor prompts differ from tutorials in being curriculum-embedded, teacher-assessable, and tied to specific teaching events—they must be updated with lesson plans and cannot be modular or autonomous.

Anthropomorphism in AI prompts is often a 'production fallacy'—language written quickly that projects human capacities (rapport, authentic interest, identity) onto the AI, which then fails to deliver because those capacities are genuinely unavailable.

The practical fix is to reframe the AI as 'an audience with extremely limited capabilities,' instructing it to perform rather than feel engagement, and to name precisely what it should do in each interaction.
AI's actual strength—sentiment analysis, probabilistic pattern recognition in live language—can be exploited explicitly in mentor prompts rather than approximated through anthropomorphic instruction.

The mentor/tutorial distinction has direct classroom implications: AI can scaffold a Skinnerian drill sequence reliably; it cannot sustain a Socratic seminar in which the mentor's genuine presence matters.
quotes: Mentor prompts are embedded with teacher-assessable purposes and tuned specifically to the writing task unfolding during a particular teaching event on a particular calendar at a live school and must be updated along with lesson plans.
I must have slipped into anthropomorphism not as a design principle but as a prompt production fallacy.
The guideline? Do not ask of a bot something that is absolutely outside its training data.

Envisioning the bot as an audience with extremely limited capabilities has been helpful, communicating at every turn to the AI that the AI is not a human and must not slip into language patterns which are ambiguous on this point.
Tutorials are topic or skill driven, more akin to Skinner boxes than Socratic seminars, modular and autonomous.
My instructions in Mentor prompts now are immunized from inadvertent anthropomorphism to the degree I perceive it.
